In brief

"Professor MacHugh," central to Aeolus but encountered nowhere else in the novel except for a momentary (and hallucinatory) appearance in Circe, is a fictional version of Hugh Aloysius MacNeill, a classics scholar who, as his life went on, spent more and more time lounging in newspaper offices. He represents a time in the life of Dublin when many adult males were either unemployed or underemployed, and a time in the life of universities when an undergraduate degree in the classics still meant something. Joyce makes him embody both quirky scholarly brilliance and slow, sad decay. MacHugh is the first of several vividly portrayed eccentrics in Ulysses, and one of many Dubliners who are either treading water economically or sinking.

At more length

Joyce conveys a sense of decay through physical details. MacHugh has "frayed stained shirtcuffs," thin "claws" of fingers, and an "unshaven blackspectacled face." He munches on borrowed biscuits in the newspaper office, at one point emitting "A dumb belch of hunger," and loudly flosses his teeth in public. Lenehan's limerick about his "goggles of ebony hue" implies that he has a drinking problem: "As he mostly sees double / To wear them why trouble?" Richard Ellmann adds some consonant details about MacNeill: "Ordinarily careless in dress, he had for a time a position as teacher of romance languages at Maynooth, and so was obliged to wear hat and tailcoat; he usually left them unbrushed. Gogarty, speculating upon this garb, evidently made the remark, 'In mourning for Sallust', which passes through Stephen's mind. MacNeill used to arrive early in the morning at the Evening Telegraph offices, read the paper, and remain all day. As the members of the staff arrived, he reprimanded them for being late. The title of professor was accorded him out of slightly ironic politeness, for in fact he never attained that eminence" (289). As will become clear in a moment, that judgment is not entirely true.

Vivien Igoe, in Real People, and John Simpson, in a long series of essays on JJON, have have uncovered many more facts about MacNeill's life. He was born in Glenarm, in northeast Ireland's Glens of Antrim, in 1866. His family was ambitious, and he and his three brothers all seem to have been blessed with intelligence. The youngest brother, Eion (christened John), became particularly successful: he co-founded the Gaelic League, built a strong reputation as a scholar of medieval Irish history, worked for Irish independence in the years leading up to the Easter Rising without endorsing bloodshed, and later held political offices in the Free State. Hugh was a good student, but slightly less spectacular than his younger brother. After obtaining his BA he began a career as a teacher, with some claim to the title "professor," but his professional career traced a steady downward trajectory. Igoe quotes the judgment of a dismayed but admiring comrade: "He did not much care for getting on in the world; indeed, his quixotic disinteredness was the despair of his friends; it seemed as though on principle he acted in opposition to his interests. Such men are rare and are, therefore, the more attractive."

Simpson quotes similar assessments from others: "Often he was a sore trial to the best of his friends, but in him was some indefinable quality that won their affection and esteem, even in his most difficult moments"; "I am awed to think that when I talked or supped with that tall, stooped, shaggy, gaunt glensman, whose beard waved wild in the wind around Dublin’s streets, I was partaking of intellectual treasures garnered nearly a century ago. His knowledge and his memory were amazing, and there was no subject, however recondite, which anybody could bring up in talk with him but MacNeill could say something interesting, fresh and illuminating upon it"; "He would argue with you for hours (if you were sufficiently foolish to try dialectical conclusions with him) on some abstruse point of Latin or French grammar. There are few men whom I have known in my life for whom I have had a greater respect as an intellect, or a greater affection as a friend"; "The memory of the Professor, in the clothes which always seemed to have been snatched up and worn almost haphazard, the long beard which, in his later years, grew so unkempt, and the wild, the splendid forehead, and the smile which lit up the rugged features when he hailed a friend, will remain with me as long as memory lasts."

In adolescence Hugh went to school in Maynooth and then (like Joyce) to Dublin's Belvedere College, where he did well. He earned admission to University College Dublin and did well there too in his first year, but after that transferred to University College, Blackrock and took a year longer than some classmates to finish. After graduating with a BA in Latin and Greek in 1888 he quickly won a place on the UCD teaching staff, instructing beginning students in Latin, Greek, and French. At first he was accorded the title of "professor" rather than merely "tutor," but this does not seem to have lasted for more than a year or two. As work at UCD became intermittent, MacNeill earned money as an examiner for the Royal University, a degree-granting organization that did not offer classes. In 1893 he and two other classicists, advertising themselves as "Professors," posted an ad in the Freeman's Journal offering to tutor students planning to take the Royal University examinations. Other entrepreneurial efforts kept him afloat into the late 1890s.

MacNeill married in 1896, and by 1900 the couple had moved into a fairly grand house called Aberdelgie on the Harbour Road in Howth. But he had serious money troubles by this time, and his financial woes only deepened in later years. When he found teaching jobs at UCD in the first two decades of the 20th century, it was as a mere "assistant." He found a position as "lecturer" at Maynooth in 1909, but this did not last more than a year or two. Increasingly he was to be found hanging out in newspaper offices—the Freeman's Journal and Evening Telegraph at first (Joyce may have found him there when he visited Ireland in 1909), and later the Irish Times. He was not employed by these papers, though the clipping from the Irish Times reproduced here identifies him posthumously as its "Chess Correspondent." He drank the tea brewed in the newsmen's offices and nibbled on their buns and biscuits.

The rest of his life's story does not bear on events in Ulysses, but it was bleak. In 1913 MacHugh could not pay his income taxes and served time as a debtor at Mountjoy Prison. During and after his release relatives had to help support his wife Mary and their four children. Little is known of their marriage in later life (Mary outlived him by one year), but by the 1930s MacNeill reportedly was sleeping at night either in the offices of the Times or in a telephone kiosk (one of the few in town) on College Green. He died in 1935 in the South Dublin Union Workhouse, a home for paupers on James's Street. 

Based on the little information he had, Ellmann judged MacNeill to be "clever and lazy." This does not seem altogether wrong, but much more can be said. "Clever" understates the man's mental energy. He seems to have been a passionate teacher, eager conversationalist, and quirky public intellectual for whom scholarly rigor was paramount. His knowledge of Latin literature was impressive, and Aeolus suggests that he loved Greek even more. He devoured newspapers and was often seen lugging about armfuls of French ones. He was also a formidable chess player. Joyce gave his character MacHugh some sharply intelligent comments and paid him the high honor of letting him recite, verbatim and from memory, the speech of John F. Taylor that, alone of all the outstanding writing in Ulysses, the author chose to record for gramophone.

As for "lazy," MacNeill clearly fell short of his potential, but many explanations seem possible: alcoholism or mental illness, perhaps, or that fatal idealism that keeps itinerant professors of the humanities pursuing poorly paying teaching jobs year after year. One likely factor is the "difficult" personality that even MacNeill's friends found a "sore trial." Aeolus shows an abrasive side to MacHugh as he responds "gruffly" to the newsboys and physically ejects one from the office. Confronted with such testiness, employers may have found it easiest simply to wash their hands of him. An office parasite who reproaches employees for arriving late may seem hilarious from a distance, but up close it was probably less funny.

Joyce made Hugh MacNeill into Professor MacHugh, converting the man's given name into a surname. Lest anyone mistake the game he was playing, he tipped his hand in Sirens, where Lenehan tells Simon Dedalus that the audience for his son's lunchtime performance included "The ponderous pundit, Hugh MacHugh."

John Hunt 2026
